paragraphs: The strongest is never strong enough to stay master forever, unless he turns strength into right and obedience into duty. From this comes the right of the strongest, a phrase that seems to be meant ironically yet is actually laid down as a basic principle. But will no one ever explain it to us? Force is a physical power, and I do not see what moral effect it could have. Yielding to force is an act of necessity, not of will — at most, an act of prudence. In what sense could it be a duty?

Suppose for a moment that this so-called “right” exists. I maintain that the only result is a heap of inexplicable nonsense. If force creates right, the effect changes along with the cause: any force greater than the first takes over its right. Once people can disobey without being punished, disobedience is legitimate. And since the strongest is always in the right, the only thing that matters is to make oneself the strongest. But what sort of right disappears when force fails? If we have to obey because we are forced, there is no need to obey because we ought to. And if we are not forced to obey, we have no obligation to. Clearly, then, the word “right” adds nothing to force. Here it means nothing at all.

Obey the powers that be. If this means yield to force, it is good advice but unnecessary, since I can promise it will never be broken. I admit that all power comes from God, but so does all sickness. Does that mean we are forbidden to call a doctor? A brigand surprises me at the edge of a wood. Am I merely forced to hand over my purse, or, even if I could keep it back, am I bound in conscience to give it up? After all, the pistol he holds is also a power.
So let us grant that force does not create right, and that we owe obedience only to legitimate powers. If so, we are back at my original question.
